AutoCUSUM: Robust Unsupervised Thresholding for Anomaly Detection on Data Streams

Jorge Casajús-Setién · Pedro Larrañaga · Concha Bielza

Abstract

We introduce AutoCUSUM, a sequential decision layer for score-based anomaly detection in data streams, designed to address the limitations of pointwise methods such as streaming Peaks-Over-Threshold (SPOT). Whereas SPOT and related approaches rely on labeled data or prior assumptions on anomaly rates, AutoCUSUM automatically learns the parameters of a CUSUM chart from normal (non-anomalous) data, resulting in a fully unsupervised pipeline. We design parameter selection as a multi-objective optimization problem grounded in information theory, with carefully constructed objectives and a principled search space. By leveraging CUSUM evidence accumulation, the proposed method attains both robustness to noise and sensitivity to sustained shifts, while producing compact, episode-level alarms that lead to a more actionable alert stream.

We evaluate AutoCUSUM on six public time-series benchmarks, including an industrial network intrusion detection case study, and compare it against SPOT. Across scenarios, AutoCUSUM consistently achieves stronger detection performance and substantially reduces false positives and alarm fragmentation. These results demonstrate that fully unsupervised calibration of sequential decision rules can outperform standard thresholding techniques while producing alerts better aligned with operational monitoring requirements.

Keywords — anomaly detection, online thresholding, time-series analysis, sequential decision making, data streams, unsupervised learning, network intrusion detection

Introduction

The Problem with Anomaly Detection in Data Streams

A widely adopted approach to anomaly detection involves learning a model of normal behavior and assigning each observation a real-valued anomaly score—a scalar that quantifies deviation from the learned norm [79]. Turning these scores into actionable alarms requires a decision rule. This step does not need anomaly labels per se. For example, MERLIN and discord discovery using matrix profiles can identify anomalous subsequences retrospectively from the complete observed sequence, without requiring a target alarm rate [12, 13].

Streaming operation, however, imposes an additional constraint: each alarm decision must be made using only the observations available at that time. Procedures that rely on the complete sequence therefore cannot be applied. The decision rule must instead be calibrated from a finite historical sample. Statistical approaches such as peaks over threshold (POT) estimate alarm thresholds from an unlabeled sample but require the user to specify a target alarm rate [10]. This parameter encodes an a priori target for alarm frequency, whether justified by operational requirements, calibrated empirically, or selected heuristically. Its streaming extensions, namely SPOT and DSPOT [10], update the tail model online but still require a user-specified target alarm rate. More generally, published works often select decision parameters using labeled anomalies, aiming to maximize test-set performance [78].

Even when the scoring model is trained without labels, tuning the subsequent decision rule using labeled anomalies reintroduces supervision into the detection pipeline. Because these examples may not represent future incidents [79], adjusting the rule to their score magnitudes and temporal patterns can weaken robustness to unseen anomalies. Operational deployment imposes practical requirements on converting an anomaly score stream into a sequence of binary anomaly labels. When large streams are monitored continuously, even a low false-positive rate can produce a substantial investigation workload [58]. A single incident may also generate intermittent score excursions, leading to repeated alarm episodes under pointwise thresholding. Suppressing short-lived fluctuations can reduce nuisance alerts but may also delay detection or obscure brief incidents.

A practical decision rule must therefore balance prompt detection, false-alarm burden, and the consolidation of related evidence into coherent alarm episodes. To preserve the unsupervised nature of the pipeline, this trade-off must be calibrated without optimizing against observed detection delays or missed-detection rates, whose direct measurement requires labeled anomalies. Additionally, this removes the need to collect and manually annotate anomalous examples for calibration [6]. An open challenge remains: developing decision rules for streaming anomaly detection that satisfy these operational requirements using normal data alone, without assuming prior knowledge of the anomalies to be encountered.

Sequential Evidence Accumulation for Robust Thresholding

The temporal structure of anomaly scores motivates a sequential approach to alarm generation. Rather than basing each alarm solely on an individual score, we introduce a second-stage rule that accumulates evidence across observations, allowing sustained departures from normal behavior to contribute jointly to the decision.

We propose treating the anomaly score stream as a stochastic process and monitoring it for significant shifts using a cumulative sum (CUSUM) chart, a classical method from statistical process control [18]. Instead of thresholding individual, noisy scores, CUSUM maintains a running statistic that increases when scores exceed a reference level and decreases toward zero when they fall below it, allowing small but persistent score increases to accumulate into detectable evidence [19]. These properties motivate three practical benefits:

  • Tolerance to transient fluctuations: Brief score excursions that might trigger false alarms under pointwise thresholding may subside before enough evidence accumulates to raise a CUSUM alarm. This inherent filtering effect can help limit the investigation workload in operational monitoring [58].
  • Sensitivity to sustained anomalies: Subtle but persistent increases in anomaly score can accumulate to cross the decision boundary [18], even when individual score values remain below a given pointwise threshold.
  • Consolidation of alarm episodes: The accumulated statistic can remain above the alarm threshold during brief score decreases, joining intermittent score excursions into a continuous alarm episode.

However, realizing these benefits depends on the choice of two CUSUM parameters: the reference value κ and the decision limit h. We therefore develop an automatic procedure to set them using only normal data, enabling fully unsupervised calibration of the decision rule for streaming operation.

Contributions and Paper Structure

This paper introduces AutoCUSUM, a second-stage decision layer that converts an anomaly score stream into binary anomaly labels. It consists of a CUSUM chart equipped with an automatic procedure for calibrating its reference value and decision limit. Using a finite sample of normal scores, the procedure optimizes a trade-off between sensitivity proxies and false-alarm penalties, without anomaly labels or a user-specified target alarm rate. We evaluate the method across different scoring models and datasets, comparing it with alternative decision rules using observation-level detection metrics, false-alarm episode counts, and detection delay.

Section II reviews related work on anomaly detection and sequential decision rules. Section III presents AutoCUSUM and its calibration procedure. Sections IV and V describe the experimental protocol and report the results, respectively. Section VI concludes the paper and outlines future work.

Related work and background

The Modeling Paradigms for Streaming Anomaly Detection

Learning normal behavior without anomaly labels is particularly relevant when future deviations cannot be characterized in advance, as with zero-day attacks in cybersecurity. Observations can then be scored by their departure from normality, without requiring examples of the anomalies to be encountered [79]. Several modeling families follow this approach. Probabilistic methods score observations through their likelihood under a reference distribution, whereas distance- and density-based methods quantify separation from neighboring observations or relative local sparsity. Reconstruction and forecasting models instead derive scores from discrepancies between observed values and reconstructed or predicted values [28].

For sequential data, recurrent networks and transformers can incorporate temporal context when reconstructing or predicting observations [28]. Their architectures and training objectives differ, but both can provide a score stream to a downstream decision rule. The scoring model is therefore treated here as an upstream component rather than the object of the proposed calibration procedure.

This distinction also matters when interpreting reported performance. Threshold-independent metrics such as the area under the ROC curve assess score ranking but do not specify an operational rule for generating anomaly labels. Conversely, an F_1 score obtained by maximizing performance over thresholds on the labeled test set evaluates an operating point selected using information unavailable under normal-only calibration [78]. Comparing decision rules therefore requires keeping the score stream fixed and distinguishing evaluation with anomaly labels from calibration without them.

Unsupervised Thresholding for Anomaly Scores

The challenge of converting continuous anomaly scores into discrete labels has motivated a range of thresholding strategies under normal-only calibration [39]. While thresholds can be tuned in a supervised manner when labeled anomalies are available—for example, by maximizing F_1 or selecting an operating point from the ROC curve—the central difficulty in streaming anomaly detection lies in selecting a robust decision boundary from normal data alone. Simple unsupervised approaches apply summary statistics to the score distribution, such as k-sigma rules [40] or high-percentile cutoffs [41]. However, these methods implicitly assume specific score distributions (often Gaussian), rely on arbitrary parameter choices, and are highly sensitive to how representative the calibration sample is of the system’s normal operating behavior. This issue is exacerbated in streaming settings where the long-term score distribution is unknown a priori.

To better model the tail of the score distribution where rare events occur, extreme value theory (EVT) has been adapted to threshold selection. EVT-based methods, such as POT and SPOT, model exceedances above an initial high threshold using a generalized Pareto distribution and derive the final decision boundary from a user-specified high quantile of the fitted tail, thereby enforcing an acceptable rate of extreme events [10]. In practice, their primary bottleneck lies in the choice of the initial threshold: it must be high enough for EVT asymptotics to hold, yet low enough to yield sufficient exceedances for stable parameter estimation [42]. Existing selection procedures either rely on subjective diagnostics [43], simple heuristics such as fixed empirical quantiles [44], or more automated schemes that introduce additional parameters and complexity [45, 46]. As a result, a fully automatic, robust, and assumption-light procedure for setting this threshold from normal data alone remains elusive.

Notably, even systems with strong score-level separability can underperform in practice when paired with suboptimal or heuristic thresholds [47], underscoring that effective anomaly detection requires decision parameters to be derived from normal data alone rather than anomaly examples, strong assumptions, or subjective choices.

CUSUM for Change and Anomaly Detection

CUSUM [18] is a sequential change-detection technique from statistical process control that accumulates deviations from a target value over time. Unlike Shewhart charts [48], which evaluate observations independently, CUSUM integrates evidence over time. This cumulative formulation attenuates the effect of isolated spikes or transient noise, reducing false alarms from fluctuations, yet remains sensitive to small but persistent shifts in the process mean [19]. Changes in the monitored process appear as a distinct variation in the slope of the CUSUM trace, making them intuitive to identify.

In its standard formulation, a CUSUM chart is governed by two parameters: a reference value κ, which determines the extent to which deviations contribute to the accumulated evidence, and a decision limit h, which specifies when the accumulated statistic is sufficient to trigger an alarm [49]. Together, these parameters govern the trade-off between sensitivity to anomalies and false-alarm rate, and thus have a strong influence on detection performance. Classical CUSUM designs select (κ,h) based on average run length (ARL) criteria, where ARL denotes the expected number of samples until the chart raises an alarm [50]. Accordingly, the ARL is intended to be long when the monitored process operates under normal conditions, so that false alarms are rare, and short once a change has occurred, so that deviations are detected quickly.

Because CUSUM is sensitive to sustained shifts while filtering transient spikes, it is widely used for online monitoring across domains, including manufacturing quality control [49], industrial fault detection [51], and network intrusion monitoring [52]. Its cumulative nature makes it a natural complement to sequence models that produce context-aware anomaly scores, yielding a stable sequential decision rule. Despite this potential, the use of CUSUM as a general post-processing layer for anomaly detection—monitoring the anomaly-score stream from an upstream model—is mostly untapped, and existing studies consistently expose a parameterization challenge. For example, prior work has coupled a recurrent neural network with a CUSUM chart [53], but selected κ empirically and relied on visual inspection for anomaly judgment. Similarly, CUSUM has also been applied to transformer-generated scores [54], albeit with only partial calibration: κ was tuned from local means, but h remained heuristically chosen.

Methodology: From Scores to Labels

We propose a two-stage framework for streaming anomaly detection, illustrated in Figure 1. In Stage 1, an unsupervised detector processes the input data stream and produces a continuous anomaly score stream. Stage 2 is AutoCUSUM, our proposed sequential decision module, which converts the score stream into binary anomaly labels using a calibrated CUSUM chart. The two CUSUM parameters are estimated from a finite sample of normal behavior and then fixed for online operation. The following subsections describe each stage.

Stage 1: Anomaly Score Generation

The scoring block is trained exclusively on normal data and must condense the temporal structure of the input stream x_1, x_2, …, with x_t ∈ 𝕀R^n, into reliable scalar anomaly scores at each time step. Accordingly, the proposed framework is compatible with any unsupervised scoring model that assigns a scalar score per time step. In practical anomaly detection systems, raw model outputs are typically transformed via a monotonic mapping so that scores are ordered by anomalousness, with larger values indicating stronger deviations from normal behavior. Therefore, without loss of generality, we assume anomaly scores to be non-negative, s_t ∈ 𝕀R_+.

For parallelizable scoring models without explicit state recurrence, temporal context is typically incorporated by applying the detector to sliding windows of the input stream. Specifically, at each time step t, the scorer operates on a window W_t = x_t-m+1, …, x_t of fixed length m and associates the resulting score s_t with the most recent observation x_t.

Att(Q,K,V) = softmax ((QK^⊤)/(√(d_k)))V,

where the softmax is applied row-wise and the scaling factor √(d_k) stabilizes gradients. Within each encoder and decoder layer, scaled dot-product attention is applied to aggregate information across the layer input. This corresponds to the case where the same input is provided as queries, keys, and values to the attention mechanism (Q = K = V), and is denoted self-attention. Decoder layers additionally apply encoder–decoder (cross) attention, in which the queries are taken from the decoder internal state, while keys and values are taken from the encoder outputs, allowing the decoder to integrate contextual information extracted by the encoder.

Loss(W_i) = big\|x_i+1-D(W_i,E(W_i))big\|.

The model is trained on normal data by minimizing this loss over all windows. After training, this same quantity is used as an anomaly score, with s_i+1 = Loss(W_i) ∈ 𝕀R_+, so that windows whose continuation is poorly predicted by the learned normal dynamics yield larger scores.

Stage 2: The AutoCUSUM Decision Block

Stage 2, the AutoCUSUM decision block, constitutes the core novel contribution of this work. It maps the anomaly score stream produced by Stage 1, S = s_1, s_2, …, into a sequence of binary labels l_t ∈ 0,1, indicating normal (0) or anomalous (1) behavior. This transformation is performed using a CUSUM control chart whose parameters are automatically calibrated from normal-only data and then fixed during online deployment.

The CUSUM Transformation

c_t = max0, c_t-1 + s_t - κ,

where κ is the reference value defining the baseline score level [18]. This transformation makes the chart sensitive to persistent positive shifts, which progressively accumulate in the statistic, while remaining robust to isolated spikes that are quickly absorbed by the max0,· operation.

l_t = 1 if c_t ge h, 0 otherwise.

After an anomalous episode has been handled—either by a human operator or an automated response—the CUSUM accumulator may be reset to avoid carry-over effects and to enable detection of new, independent anomalies. Alternatively, one may choose not to reset immediately, allowing c_t to continue accumulating so that (i) its magnitude reflects the severity of the ongoing anomalous episode and (ii) more information is recovered about the anomaly by aggregating multiple anomalous instances into a single episode.

The AutoCUSUM Optimization Algorithm

The effectiveness of the decision module depends critically on the joint choice of the reference value κ and the decision limit h: poor parameter settings may lead to excessive false alarms or missed detections. AutoCUSUM addresses this challenge by automatically calibrating (κ, h) using only a sequence of anomaly scores S = s_1, s_2, …, s_T obtained from normal behavior. Calibration is performed by optimizing a suitable objective function over a constrained parameter search space.

Supervised calibration using labeled anomalies is possible but undesirable, as it biases the detector toward known anomaly types and undermines the label-free premise of unsupervised anomaly detection. Accordingly, AutoCUSUM relies exclusively on anomaly scores observed under normal behavior to set (κ, h). As a result, the objective function cannot be defined in terms of detection accuracy against known anomalies. At the same time, simply minimizing the number of alarms on normal data would lead to a trivial, non-detecting solution (e.g., h → ∞).

AutoCUSUM therefore formalizes a fundamental trade-off: selecting (κ, h) from normal-only data so as to preserve as much information as possible from the original anomaly score stream, while minimizing the expected number of false alarms. To operationalize this idea, the AutoCUSUM algorithm is organized into three main components: (i) defining the parameter search space, (ii) specifying an objective function, and (iii) optimizing this function within the defined space.

Component 1: Parameter Search Space

C(κ) = c_1(κ), c_2(κ), …, c_T(κ),

where c_t(κ) is defined recursively according to Equation (1). The AutoCUSUM optimization procedure begins by defining a principled search space for κ based on the properties of C(κ).

κ_max ≔ max_t=1,…,T s_t.
H[C(κ_max)] = - ∑_y p(C(κ_max)=y) log p(C(κ_max)=y) = p(C(κ_max)=0) log p(C(κ_max)=0)_=0 = 0.

This formally confirms that once κ reaches κ_max, the CUSUM series preserves no information about the variability of the original score sequence S, supporting κ_max as an information-theoretic upper bound for the search.

κ le κ_min ⇒ ∀ t > 0: c_t(κ) = c_t-1(κ) + s_t - κ ⇒ ∀ t > 0: s_t = c_t(κ) - c_t-1(κ) + κ.
κ > κ_min ⇒ ∃ t>0 | c_t-1(κ)+s_t-κ<0.
κ > κ_min ⇒ c_i-1(κ) + s_i - κ < 0 ⇒ big(c_i-2(κ) + s_i-1 - κbig) + s_i - κ < 0 hspace2.7em… ⇒ ∑_j=1^i (s_j - κ) < 0 ⇔ κ > (1)/(i)∑_j=1^i s_j.
κ_min = min_i=1,…,T (1)/(i)∑_j=1^i s_j.

Summarizing the above, all reference values outside [κ_min,κ_max] are equivalent: any κge κ_max yields the inert chart C(κ)≡ 0, while any κle κ_min yields a lossless linear recursion with no clipping. Consequently, any nontrivial trade-off between information preservation and filtering can only arise for κ∈(κ_min,κ_max).

h_max(κ)=max_t=1,…,T c_t(κ),

since any choice of h>h_max(κ) would trivially yield zero alarms for that specific κ.

Component 2: Objective Function

  1. Maximizing Detection Sensitivity (O_DS): the system should be effective at identifying true anomalies.
  2. Minimizing False Alarms (O_FA): the system should raise as few alarms as possible on normal data.

Table I summarizes the monotone effect of the CUSUM reference value κ and decision limit h on the objectives O_DS and O_FA: decreasing either parameter improves detection performance but increases false alarms, whereas increasing them has the opposite effect. These monotonicities make single-objective tuning ill-posed: optimizing only O_DS collapses to the trivial extreme (κ_min, h_min), while optimizing only O_FA yields (κ_max, h_max). We therefore construct a vector-valued objective J(κ,h) capturing competing criteria for detection performance and false alarms. In the following, we introduce candidate objective terms to represent O_DS and O_FA, and we discuss the ablations of their combinations in Section \mbox {V-A.

To incorporate O_DS into J(κ,h) in our unsupervised setting, direct evaluation is not possible, as it would require labeled anomaly data. Instead, under the working assumption that increased informativeness correlates with a higher probability of detecting true anomalies, we rely on the following proxy objectives for O_DS:

  1. Differential Entropy: Each c_t(κ) is obtained through the accumulation of multiple incremental contributions along the recursion. Thus, motivated by the central limit theorem, we model the induced CUSUM series C(κ) as Gaussian with empirical mean μ(κ) and standard deviation σ(κ). We use its differential entropy [55] as a proxy objective that exerts a downward pressure on κ, as higher entropy means higher informational content: J_ent(κ) ≡ H!left(C(κ)right) = 12log!left(2π e,σ^2(κ)right).
  2. Sum of absolute log returns: To quantify the dynamic activity of the CUSUM series, we compute the sum of absolute log returns [56]. We first form a subsequence C^+(κ) by retaining only strictly positive values of C(κ) (to avoid undefined logarithms), and denote its length by M. The objective is then: J_log(κ) = ∑_t=2^M left| log c^+_t(κ) - log c^+_t-1(κ) right|. Larger values indicate stronger temporal variability in the CUSUM series, which we interpret as a proxy for higher sensitivity. Maximizing this term therefore also exerts downward pressure on κ.
  3. Parameter regularization (κ and h): As direct structural proxies for sensitivity, we penalize large values of both κ and h within their respective admissible ranges. Concretely, we minimize J_κ(κ)=κ and J_h(h)=h. This complements the information-based proxies and discourages overly conservative configurations that would hinder detection.

In parallel, to counteract the push for higher sensitivity, we introduce objective terms associated with false alarm control, O_FA. These objectives are computable using only normal data and penalize parameter choices that produce an excessive number of alarms:

  1. Number of alarms: The most direct measure of false alarms is the count of threshold crossings: J_alarm(κ, h) = ∑_t=1^T 𝕀Ibig(c_t(κ) ge hbig), where 𝕀(·) is the indicator function, equal to 1 if the condition holds and 0 otherwise. Minimizing this term directly reduces the number of false positives, creating upward pressure on both κ and h.
  2. Mean value of the CUSUM series: As a proxy for controlling false alarms, we penalize the average magnitude of the CUSUM series. A series with a lower mean is less likely to cross the threshold. This is measured as: J_mean(κ) = 1T ∑_t=1^T c_t(κ). Minimizing this term, which depends only on κ, encourages a more dampened CUSUM series and thus exerts upward pressure on κ.

Table II summarizes all the candidate objectives.

Component 3: Pareto Search

We solve the multi-objective problem under a minimization convention: objectives originally posed as maximization terms are negated. Objectives are also normalized to [0,1] over the current population. We then use a multi-objective optimization procedure to obtain an approximate Pareto set of candidate parameter pairs, denoted by P. For any (κ_i,h_i)inP, let J(κ_i,h_i)=big(J_1(κ_i,h_i),…,J_D(κ_i,h_i)big) denote the corresponding D-dimensional vector of normalized objective values, evaluated over the retained subset of objectives from Table II. We evaluate two common strategies for selecting a single parameter pair (κ,h) from P [57]:

  • Ideal Point Distance Rule: This strategy selects the parameter pair in mathcal P whose normalized objective vector is closest to the hypothetical ideal point, where all objectives would simultaneously attain their best possible value. With normalized minimization objectives, the ideal point is the origin, so the rule amounts to minimizing the ℓ_2-norm of the objective vector: (κ_ideal,h_ideal) = (κ_i,h_i)∈Pargmin big|J(κ_i,h_i)big|_2.
  • Knee Point Rule (Hyperplane Distance): We select a single compromise solution from the normalized approximate Pareto set using a distance-to-hyperplane criterion, commonly used to identify a “knee''-like trade-off point, beyond which a small improvement in one objective requires a large sacrifice in another. Let e_1,…,e_D be the standard basis vectors in the normalized objective space. These extreme points, for which one objective takes its worst value while all others take their best one, span the affine hyperplane of extreme trade-offs, Π. We select the parameter pair in mathcal P whose normalized objective vector lies farthest from it: (κ_knee,h_knee) = (κ_i,h_i)∈Pargmax dist!left(J(κ_i,h_i), Π right).

Experimental Setup

Goals and Research Questions

  1. Q1 – AutoCUSUM Setting: Which choices of candidate terms in J(κ,h), Pareto-front selection rule, and multi-objective optimization settings reliably yield an effective (κ,h) pair?
  2. Q2 – Comparative Performance: How does AutoCUSUM (using the best configuration from Q1) compare against established unsupervised thresholding baselines for data streams, in particular the SPOT method?
  3. Q3 – Model Agnosticism: How robust is AutoCUSUM when applied to anomaly scores generated by different underlying anomaly detection models?
  4. Q4 – NIDS Applicability: Beyond metric-level performance, does the two-stage framework convert anomaly scores into reliable, actionable NIDS alerts?

The following subsections describe the datasets, implementation details, baselines, and evaluation metrics used to answer these questions.

Datasets and Preprocessing

We use six public datasets both to configure AutoCUSUM (Q1) and to evaluate the resulting two-stage framework (Q2–Q4): five widely used multivariate time-series benchmarks (MSL, SMAP, PSM, SMD, and SWAT) and the WUSTL-IIoT-2021 IIoT intrusion detection dataset. The main characteristics of all datasets are summarized in Table III. To avoid biasing design choices toward the IIoT application, we use the benchmarking datasets to configure AutoCUSUM (Q1) and reserve WUSTL-IIoT-2021 for the final case study evaluation of practical NIDS alerting (Q4).

Across all datasets, input features are normalized to comparable ranges and grouped into overlapping windows of length W_len before being fed to the upstream scoring models. We treat W_len as an upstream scoring-model choice and therefore do not tune it in this work (which focuses on the AutoCUSUM decision stage). We fix W_len=100 throughout, since larger windows provided only marginal AUC-ROC gains in preliminary sweeps while substantially increasing computational cost.

Benchmark Datasets for Generalization

We use five multivariate time-series benchmarks spanning three operational domains (Table III) to study AutoCUSUM configuration (Q1), comparative performance (Q2), and model agnosticism (Q3). MSL and SMAP provide spacecraft telemetry with fault anomalies [58]; PSM [59] and SMD [60] contain large-scale server metrics with application/hardware failure anomalies; and SWAT captures water-treatment sensor/actuator traces with cyberattack anomalies [61]. These datasets allow us to test whether AutoCUSUM transfers across domains with different signal characteristics and anomaly mechanisms.

Case Study: IIoT Network Intrusion Detection

Industry 4.0 and IIoT have driven massive connectivity in industrial networks, increasing both traffic volume and exposure to sophisticated attacks [63]. As traditional signature-based approaches often fall short in this setting, AI-driven anomaly detection is a natural fit [64]. However, practical NIDS deployment makes the thresholding problem particularly acute, as highlighted in our previous transformer-based NIDS work [17]. While the model produced high-quality anomaly scores, operational deployment requires converting them into reliable alerts to avoid downtime and alert fatigue [21], in a manner that is robust and avoids reliance on label-informed calibration and manual tuning, both of which can bias the alerting mechanism. These challenges position IIoT NIDS as an ideal testbed for our two-stage framework: given an upstream scoring model (here, a transformer), the AutoCUSUM decision layer must turn noisy, scale-ambiguous anomaly scores into actionable alerts under strict false-alarm constraints, leveraging the cumulative-evidence properties of CUSUM (Section \mbox {I-B).

We adopt the publicly available WUSTL-IIoT-2021 dataset [62]. To ensure a proper unsupervised setup, we construct a purely normal training set by selecting the largest continuous block with the lowest attack density and removing the remaining anomalies within that block. The rest of the data is reserved for testing. Test anomalies fall into four categories representative of industrial threats: Denial of Service (DoS) with 78,305 attack instances; Reconnaissance with 8,240; Command Injection with 259; and Backdoor with 212. To obtain a fair, attack-specific evaluation, we partition the test set into four sequences, each containing a single attack typology. This prevents long, high-density attacks (e.g., DoS) from triggering persistent alarms that could artificially inflate apparent detection of subtler attacks.

Implementation Details

All experiments were implemented in Python and executed on a server equipped with an Intel Xeon Gold 6538Y+ CPU, 256 GB of RAM and four NVIDIA L4 GPUs.

To generate the anomaly score streams, we used the upstream scoring models summarized in Table IV: our own implementation of the transformer reconstruction model described in Section \mbox {III-A, and a suite of models from the TSLib library [65], a PyTorch framework for deep learning on time series. For the TSLib baselines we use the off-the-shelf configuration, with input dimensionality set per-dataset to match its feature dimension. This avoids model-specific optimization, isolating the effect of the decision module.

To instantiate the multi-objective optimization procedure, we use NSGA-II [75], an evolutionary algorithm based on non-dominated sorting and crowding-distance preservation, implemented through the pymoo library [76]. Composite objective candidates are formed by combining the scalar objectives in Table II, retaining only combinations that induce both upward and downward pressure on each parameter (κ and h), yielding 15 valid objectives. To configure AutoCUSUM (Q1), we run a grid search over the candidate composite objectives, the Pareto-front selector, and the optimizer hyperparameters—population size (candidates per generation), tolerance (improvement threshold for declaring convergence), and stopping criterion (whether convergence is measured in parameter space or objective space)—as specified in Table V. Each run is capped at 50,000 objective evaluations. Results for each experimental condition (dataset, scoring model, configuration) are averaged over five random seeds.

Baselines and Evaluation Protocol

With the AutoCUSUM configuration fixed, we turn to the remaining research questions. To address Q2 and Q3, AutoCUSUM is compared against SPOT across all benchmark datasets (Table III) and across all upstream models from the TSLib benchmark suite (Table IV). To address Q4 we use the WUSTL-IIoT-2021 cybersecurity case study, with the transformer model from our previous work [17] serving as the scoring block of our two-stage pipeline. On this fixed score stream, the decision block is instantiated either as AutoCUSUM or as SPOT, enabling a direct comparison under identical upstream conditions.

To the best of our knowledge, no fully unsupervised threshold calibration framework is currently available for streaming anomaly scores. We nevertheless adopt SPOT [14] as the baseline because it is the closest established online thresholding method to our setting: rather than relying intrinsically on labeled anomalies, it calibrates thresholds through an EVT model. However, SPOT requires the specification of a risk parameter r, which determines the target false-alarm rate. In practice, this can be done either by imposing prior assumptions on the tail behavior or the acceptable alarm level, or by calibrating r from labeled data. For the purposes of comparison, we adopt the latter strategy and tune r using ground truth labels, searching over r∈[10^-6,10^-2] on a log-spaced grid, and selecting r=10^-5 as the value that maximizes mean performance averaged across the five benchmarks. This gives SPOT oracle-level visibility into the anomaly rate and provides a strong reference point under favorable calibration conditions. In contrast, AutoCUSUM is configured without access to anomaly labels and without tuning any parameter that explicitly controls the false-alarm rate.

Throughout the experiments, we use labeled ground truth and adopt an episode-based reset policy. After each true anomaly at time t, we schedule a CUSUM reset at t+W_len; if another anomaly occurs before that time, the reset is postponed. Thus, the accumulator is reset to zero only after a full anomaly-free window of length W_len has elapsed. This treats dense clusters of anomalies as a single extended incident, emulating an in-the-loop response process, while ensuring that anomalies separated by at least W_len normal samples are evaluated as independent detection events. We then evaluate the detection/false-alarm trade-off using metrics tailored to the temporal structure of each dataset:

  • Benchmarking datasets: Evaluation is carried out over individual timestamps, since anomalies in these datasets are typically sporadic. We report F_1 as the primary summary metric, reflecting the balance between missed detections and false alarms.
  • WUSTL-IIoT case study: Anomalies in this dataset occur as sustained attack tracks. Thus, we define two track-based evaluation metrics that, to the best of our knowledge, are novel in this application domain. The track detection rate (TDR) is the fraction of timestamps within an attack track that are flagged as anomalous. The false alarm rate (FAR) is computed only over the normal windows surrounding each attack track, since intermediate timestamps during an ongoing attack cannot be rigorously classified as normal.

Results

Optimal AutoCUSUM Configuration (Q1)

To interpret the results of this joint grid, we first aggregate performance at the level of candidate composite objectives. Table VI reports per-dataset mean F_1 for the four best candidates. Over 5 datasets, 10 models, and 48 matched configurations (2,400 paired instances), the composite objective (J_ent, J_log, J_mean, J_h, J_alarm) improves F_1 by 0.023 on average relative to the mean across all objectives, with a paired Cohen's d=0.63 computed on paired differences (SD of differences: 0.037). The difference to the second-best candidate, (J_ent, J_log, J_h, J_alarm), is negligible (mean difference: 0.0012; SD of differences: 0.045). Although one might expect this four-term objective to be noticeably cheaper to optimize, the measured runtimes of the two best composite objectives are nearly indistinguishable. Hence, we adopt (J_ent, J_log, J_mean, J_h, J_alarm) as the default composite objective, while noting that the four-term variant remains an almost cost-equivalent, slightly simpler alternative.

Having selected the composite objective, we examine the remaining design choices via marginal and conditional ablations over the full grid. When pooling all grid points, population size is the only factor producing a noticeable change in mean F_1: a population of 100 achieves barF_1 ≈ 0.815, while the next best setting attains barF_1 ≈ 0.809 (SD ≈ 0.11). The remaining factors exhibit essentially flat effects. Conditioned on this population size, the Pareto selector becomes the dominant choice: the knee-point rule achieves barF_1 ≈ 0.823 versus barF_1 ≈ 0.807 for the ideal-point distance rule (SD ≈ 0.11). Setting the selection rule to knee-point, the remaining settings lie on a clear plateau. Varying the stopping rule or tolerance changes barF_1 by at most ≈ 0.003, which is negligible relative to the dispersion scale (SD ≈ 0.11). We therefore select these remaining hyperparameters on practical grounds, adopting a less strict tolerance and the objective-space stopping criterion, which empirically behaves more reliably in this tolerance regime; this choice is further supported by the fact that the best-performing configuration in the full grid search corresponds to this same setting. The resulting configuration is reported in Table VII and used in all subsequent experiments (Q2–Q4).

Comparative Performance Against SPOT (Q2)

Table VIII compares AutoCUSUM against SPOT at the dataset level, with SPOT calibrated under the oracle protocol defined in Section \mbox {IV-D. AutoCUSUM attains higher mean F_1 on four out of five datasets (MSL, SMAP, PSM, and SWAT), while SPOT performs best only on SMD.

Across the 50 dataset–model pairs, AutoCUSUM improves F_1 over SPOT in 70\% of cases. Let Delta F_1 denote the per-pair F_1 difference (AutoCUSUM minus SPOT). Under the hypothesis that AutoCUSUM achieves higher F_1 than SPOT, we perform a paired sign-flip permutation test over the 50 paired differences, estimated via Monte Carlo with B=5,000,000 random sign patterns and using the plus-one estimator p_+=(k+1)/(B+1) to avoid zero p-values under finite Monte Carlo sampling, yielding p_+≈ 3× 10^-6. Because F_1 values computed for different models on the same dataset share a common data source, they cannot be treated as independent observations. We therefore also analyze the effect at the dataset level by averaging Delta F_1 across models within each dataset and applying bootstrap over these summaries. We compute the exact bootstrap distribution by enumerating all 3,125 ordered resamples obtained by sampling the five dataset-level summaries with replacement. This yields a mean dataset-level improvement of 0.0396 with a 95% bootstrap confidence interval of (0.0047, 0.0826), which supports a positive dataset-level effect in favor of AutoCUSUM. Note that SPOT is evaluated under the oracle risk-calibration protocol described in Section \mbox {IV-D. Its reported performance should therefore be interpreted as an optimistic upper bound under fully unsupervised deployment, whereas AutoCUSUM operates without any label-informed calibration.

Model-Agnostic Performance Across Scoring Models (Q3)

We now address Q3 by shifting the analysis to the scoring-model dimension. Specifically, we evaluate whether AutoCUSUM still exhibits a consistent advantage over SPOT across different anomaly scoring models, independently of the dataset on which they are applied. Figure 2 presents box plots of the resulting F_1 distributions for each scoring model. Each box summarizes variability across datasets and seeds, isolating the interaction between the thresholding strategy and the underlying anomaly score.

AutoCUSUM achieves higher mean F_1 than SPOT in 9 out of 10 scoring models when averaging over datasets and seeds, indicating that the gains observed in Q2 are not driven by a favorable alignment with a small subset of scorers. Figure 3 presents illustrative violin plots of normalized anomaly-score distributions for three representative scoring models: FEDformer, Film, and Transformer. Despite pronounced differences in multimodality (multiple density peaks at different score levels), skewness, and tail behavior, AutoCUSUM maintains consistent performance across these heterogeneous scoring regimes, suggesting that its optimization-driven calibration adapts effectively to heterogeneous scoring dynamics.

These results support the conclusion that the performance advantage of AutoCUSUM over SPOT is largely model agnostic, validating its suitability as a drop-in thresholding mechanism across diverse anomaly detection pipelines.

Analysis of Practical Applicability Improvements (Q4)

Building on the sequential-evidence accumulation advantages discussed in Section \mbox {I-B, we evaluate whether AutoCUSUM produces alarm episodes that better match operational monitoring needs than pointwise SPOT detections. Using WUSTL-IIoT-2021 as our case study, we feed anomaly scores from our transformer-based NIDS scorer [17] into both methods. We compare practical behavior qualitatively via strip plots of the resulting alarm streams and quantitatively using the track-based protocol in Section \mbox {IV-D. Table IX reports FAR and TDR across the four attack scenarios in the dataset.

The DoS scenario is the only case in Table IX in which AutoCUSUM is not Pareto-dominant: it achieves near-perfect detection of the attack track, but incurs a slightly higher false-alarm rate than SPOT. Importantly, at a comparable FAR scale, SPOT is markedly more conservative, detecting the attack only partially. To further illustrate these results, Figure 4 contains a visual representation of the alarms set off both by AutoCUSUM and SPOT on the DoS scenario. A closer inspection reveals that this apparent trade-off is largely an artifact: AutoCUSUM triggers a single consolidated alarm episode, whereas SPOT produces over three hundred non-contiguous threshold exceedances, of which 46 occur outside the attack window (false positives). Thus, despite its slightly higher FAR under the track-based protocol, AutoCUSUM yields a substantially more usable alert stream, while the fragmented point-wise detections provided by SPOT would impose markedly higher analyst workload.

Conclusion

We introduced AutoCUSUM, a fully unsupervised framework to convert anomaly scores into actionable alarms.

For Q1, we conducted an extensive grid search to assess the sensitivity of AutoCUSUM to the configuration of its components. Results indicate that, once the composite objective is fixed, performance is largely robust to the optimizer hyperparameters and the Pareto-front selection rule. For Q2–Q3, we showed that AutoCUSUM exceeds the close-to-unsupervised streaming SPOT baseline across multiple benchmark datasets and anomaly scoring models, supporting its model-agnostic applicability. For Q4, we demonstrated operational relevance in industrial cybersecurity: on WUSTL-IIoT-2021, AutoCUSUM achieves strong detection with minimal false alarms while producing consolidated alarm episodes.

  • eliminates reliance on label-informed calibration,
  • converts pointwise detections into compact alarm episodes that reduce analyst workload, and
  • generalizes robustly to unseen attack scenarios.

Several limitations point to clear opportunities for improvement. AutoCUSUM is more computationally demanding than SPOT during offline optimization, since its parameters are obtained through repeated multi-objective optimization. Notably, this cost is confined to the calibration stage: online deployment reduces to a fixed scalar CUSUM recurrence and a threshold comparison at each time step, whereas SPOT must maintain and update an EVT model during streaming operation. A further limitation is that the current CUSUM formulation uses sample order only and does not explicitly model irregular sampling intervals, potentially leaving temporal information unexploited. Finally, AutoCUSUM currently uses fixed parameters and may be suboptimal under non-stationary data. Motivated by these limitations, we identify the following directions for future research:

  • Hybrid AutoCUSUM+SPOT: develop a combined scheme that jointly optimizes the CUSUM reference parameter κ and the SPOT risk level parameter, removing supervised prevalence assumptions while leveraging complementary persistence- and peak-based detection.
  • Time-aware AutoCUSUM: add explicit time information, following time-adaptive CUSUM variants [77].
  • Operational deployment: integrate AutoCUSUM into streaming NIDS and evaluate it with human-in-the-loop studies focusing on usability, scalability, and trust. In particular, quantify whether operators respond more effectively when presented with an aggregated alarm stream rather than raw anomaly scores.
  • Dynamic AutoCUSUM: extend the framework to adapt AutoCUSUM under distribution shift, enabling continuous online recalibration.
